summary: Specifies the GSS-API authentication method for SOCKS version 5, including encapsulation that gives integrity, authentication and optional confidentiality. It is on the standards track as a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: This lets the SOCKS doorman use a general security system to check who you are and protect your messages.

questions: what is gss-api authentication for socks
how does socks5 gss-api authentication work
what are the socks5 gss-api protection levels
what is the socks5 gss-api message format
subtitle: How a SOCKS version 5 client and server prove who they are and protect traffic using GSS-API.

tldr.problem: SOCKS version 5 has a framework for plugging in authentication methods, but needs a concrete method that gives strong authentication, integrity and optional confidentiality.
tldr.mechanism: The client and server establish a GSS-API security context by swapping tokens in framed messages, agree a protection level, and then wrap all further TCP and UDP traffic with the GSS-API per-message protection calls.
tldr.outcome: SOCKS V5 can use any GSS-API security mechanism for authentication and message protection, and the protection offered depends entirely on that mechanism.

facts.label: Message types
facts.value: 1 auth, 2 protection level, 3 user data, 0xff abort

today: RFC 1961 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of the GSS-API method for SOCKS V5 described in RFC 1928.

sections.title: Purpose and Approach
sections.content:
The SOCKS Version 5 specification (RFC 1928) defines a general framework for using arbitrary authentication protocols when a connection is first set up. RFC 1961 supplies one such method: the GSS-API authentication method. It also defines an encapsulation that provides integrity, authentication and optional confidentiality.

GSS-API is an abstract interface that offers security services to distributed applications while hiding the specific security mechanism underneath. It is specified in RFC 1508 and RFC 1509. Two peers interoperate by agreeing on a common mechanism, either by administrative action or by negotiation.

The approach is to authenticate client and server by successfully establishing a GSS-API security context. GSS-API itself handles any negotiation of the mechanism and of the security service options. The per-message protection calls are then used to wrap all further TCP and UDP traffic between client and server.
sections.eli5: Instead of inventing its own way to check IDs, SOCKS borrows a general ID-checking toolkit. Once the IDs are checked, everything the two sides say is sealed in envelopes.

sections.title: Establishing the Security Context
sections.content:
Before using any GSS-API calls, client and server should be locally authenticated and have default GSS-API credentials. The client calls gss_import_name to turn the server name into an internal form. It should use the default name type GSS_C_NULL_OID and treat the name string as opaque. With Kerberos V5 naming the name may look like SERVICE:socks@socks_server_hostname, but other mechanisms may use other forms, so the client should not assume a syntax.

The client then calls gss_init_sec_context, typically passing the default credential, the default mechanism, a null context and the imported server name. The client must always request mutual authentication, replay protection, delegation and sequence protection by passing GSS_C_MUTUAL_FLAG | GSS_C_REPLAY_FLAG | GSS_C_DELEG_FLAG | GSS_C_SEQUENCE_FLAG. However, GSS_C_SEQUENCE_FLAG should be passed only by TCP-based clients, not UDP-based ones.

If the call returns GSS_S_CONTINUE_NEEDED, the client expects a token from the server in the next reply, feeds it into another call, and repeats until the continue operations are done. If it returns GSS_S_COMPLETE, the client sends any resulting output token to the server. If there is no output token, it goes on to send its protected request details. If GSS-API fails during initialisation, the client must close its connection.

On the server, the client's token is passed to gss_accept_sec_context as input. On the first call the context handle is GSS_C_NO_CONTEXT and the credential is GSS_C_NO_CREDENTIAL for default acceptor credentials. The server returns any output token to the client and keeps going on a continue result. If the call completes with no token to return, the server sends a zero-length token to signal that it is ready to receive the client's request.
sections.eli5: You and the doorman pass notes back and forth showing your ID cards until each of you is satisfied. If either of you fails the check, the door shuts.

sections.title: Message Framing
sections.content:
Every message in this method has a small frame: a ver field, a mtyp field, a len field giving the length of the token in octets, and then the token, which can be up to 2^16 - 1 octets. The ver value is 1 for this first version of the SOCKS/GSS-API protocol.

The message type tells what the token carries. Type 1 is an authentication message, used for the client's initial token and for the server's continue and confirmation replies. Type 2 is a protection-level negotiation message. Type 3 is encapsulated user data.

When the server refuses the connection for any reason, whether GSS-API authentication failure or otherwise, it returns a short abort message containing only ver and mtyp, where mtyp is 0xff.
sections.eli5: Every note has a label on the outside saying what kind of note it is and how long it is. A special red-stamped note means the doorman said no.

sections.title: Agreeing a Protection Level
sections.content:
Once a context exists, the peers can learn which per-message services are available from the return flags GSS_C_INTEG_FLAG (integrity) and GSS_C_CONF_FLAG (confidentiality). The protection applied should fit the sensitivity of the data and the severity of the threats.

Because different levels of protection are possible for TCP and UDP, a further subnegotiation follows. The client sends the protection level it requires, and the server answers with the level it agrees to, which may or may not take the client's request into account. The level must be one of three values:

  • 1: required per-message integrity.
  • 2: required per-message integrity and confidentiality.
  • 3: selective per-message integrity or confidentiality, based on local client and server configurations.

The RFC anticipates that most implementations will agree on level 1 or 2, because selective controls are hard to apply to messages passing through a SOCKS library.

The level travels in a type 2 message. The token is made by wrapping an octet holding the level with gss_seal()/gss_wrap() with conf_req set to FALSE, and is checked with gss_unseal()/gss_unwrap(). If the server's choice is unacceptable, the client must close its connection.
sections.eli5: Next you decide how careful to be. Either just seal the envelope so nobody can change it, or seal it and hide the writing too.

sections.title: Protecting Traffic and Closing Down
sections.content:
After the subnegotiation, TCP and UDP clients and servers must use the GSS-API wrapping functions, gss_seal()/gss_wrap() and gss_unseal()/gss_unwrap(), for all encapsulation. The default quality of protection is used, and conf_req_flag follows the agreed level. At level 1 it MUST always be FALSE. At level 2 it MUST always be TRUE. At level 3 each side decides per message from local configuration.

Each wrapped message is framed with message type 3, and its token holds the user data encapsulated by GSS-API.

The GSS-API context termination message, which gss_delete_sec_context would emit, is not used by this protocol. When the connection is closed, each peer calls gss_delete_sec_context() passing GSS_C_NO_BUFFER as the output token argument.
sections.eli5: From now on, everything you say to the doorman goes inside a sealed envelope, in the style you both chose. When you leave, each of you just tears up your own copy of the ID card.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security services provided through GSS-API depend entirely on how effective the underlying mechanisms are and on the correctness of their algorithms, protocols and implementations. Users of a GSS-API service must make sure the quality of protection that the mechanism provides is consistent with their security policy.

Where GSS-API supports negotiation, constraints on acceptable mechanisms may be imposed so that the result is suitable for authenticated firewall traversal.
sections.eli5: The envelopes are only as strong as the lock inside them, so check that your lock is good enough for what you are sending.

fields.name: ver
fields.desc: Protocol version; 1 for the first version of SOCKS/GSS-API.

fields.name: mtyp
fields.desc: Message type: 1 authentication, 2 protection level, 3 user data, 0xff abort.

fields.name: len
fields.desc: Length of the token field in octets.

items.label: Integrity
items.desc: Required per-message integrity; conf_req_flag is always FALSE.

items.label: Integrity and confidentiality
items.desc: Required per-message integrity and confidentiality; conf_req_flag is always TRUE.

items.label: Selective
items.desc: Integrity or confidentiality chosen per message from local configuration.
